headline: With one level and nothing to thread, `@yak/solid` compiles the styled component away entirely and renders faster than hand-written Solid, which still runs a function per instance.

microbench.why: One static `styled.button`, declared and used in the same module, is exactly what folding is for: `yak-solid` emits a plain element with a literal class and books 0.012 ms of lib self-time, so almost nothing of the library survives to render and what is left is Solid cloning a template. That is why it leads at 5.08M renders/s, ahead of `vanilla-solid` at 3.06M, which still calls a component function per instance. `next-yak` folds the same usage and lands at 2.11M — the same optimization over React's element creation instead of a template clone. `emotion` at 440,000 serializes the rule for every instance.

autocannon.why: The ordering survives a real HTTP server: `yak-solid` answers 2,740 req/s against 1,730 for `next-yak`, since a folded element leaves nothing per-request to do but concatenate strings. `panda` at 569 req/s resolves its style object inside every request, and `emotion` at 436 re-serializes.

attribution.why: `yak-solid` spends 0.313 ms per render with 0.012 ms of lib self-time and only 0.162 ms in the framework — a folded element barely enters Solid's component machinery. `vanilla-solid` books 0.275 ms of component self-time for the wrapper it keeps. `tailwind-merge` at 0.658 ms and `next-yak` at 0.672 ms arrive at the same place differently: one caches a single merge, the other folds the wrapper and still passes the class string through yak's merge, 0.294 ms of lib.

hydrate.why: `yak-solid` at 28.2 ms and `vanilla-solid` at 30.0 ms both claim the server's DOM node by node with no tree to reconcile, while every React lane rebuilds a fiber tree first and clusters near 46 ms. The gap is the framework's hydration model, not the styling library's: the two Solid lanes differ by 1.8 ms. `goober` at 134 ms injects its sheet while attaching.

inp.why: `yak-solid` at 2.3 ms and `vanilla-solid` at 2.7 ms against roughly 7.6 ms across the React lanes, but the two columns are not the same work. React re-renders with unchanged props and writes nothing to the DOM; the Solid bump changes the value every instance reads, so its bindings really do update — and a folded element with a literal class has one text node to touch.

mount.why: `yak-solid` mounts in 14.7 ms against 67.8 ms for `next-yak`. A folded element compiles to a cloned template, so the cold mount is DOM construction with no component instantiation at all; `vanilla-solid` at 17.5 ms pays 2.8 ms more for the wrapper function it keeps. `emotion` at 104 ms injects before the first paint.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation per lane. Every lane ends at one element with one class, so the style engine's work is identical and the differences live entirely in JavaScript.

payload.why: `vanilla` is the floor at 2,700 gz B, with the next-yak css-prop lanes just above at roughly 3,020 B. `yak-solid` reaches 9,031 B, and neither half of that is yak: 3,712 B is the marginal client bundle over `vanilla-solid` — the parts of `@solidjs/web` a styled component pulls in — and the rest is HTML carrying Solid's per-element `_hk` hydration key, which is unique per element and so survives gzip. The utility lanes are the heavy end, `cn` at 16,220 B and `cnfast` at 14,760 B, almost all of it library JS.

nsweep.why: `yak-solid` holds 0.771 ms at 4,000 instances, the flattest line measured, because a folded element adds nothing per instance beyond the DOM node. `emotion` at 8.63 ms and `panda-props` at 6.48 ms bend hardest.

crossCase: The floor of the depth sweep that `compose-3` and `compose-6` extend. `next-yak` holds 2.11M, 1.39M and 1.50M renders/s across the three depths, so its first wrapper costs everything and the levels after it are free. `yak-solid` starts highest of any lane at 5.08M and then falls to 241,000 and 236,000, because folding covers `styled.button` and stops at `styled(Component)`.
